items.title: 4.1 Work done by a constant force

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1 with the chapter's opening lines and Figs. 4.1 to 4.4 (PDF 75-76, printed 72-73). The learning objectives are not reproduced; the running header reads 'Work, Energy and Force'.

blocks.text: Work is often thought in terms of physical or mental effort. In Physics, however, the term work involves two things (i) force, and (ii) displacement. We shall begin with a simple situation in which work is done by a constant force.

Let us consider an object which is being pulled by a constant force F. The force displaces the object through a displacement d in the direction of force. In such a case, work W is defined as the product of the magnitude of the force F and magnitude of the displacement d. This can be written as:
Equation (4.1) shows that if displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied. For example, pushing on a wall may tire your muscles, but work done is zero as shown in Fig. 4.1.

blocks.alt: A boy leans forward and pushes a tall wall with both hands. An arrow labelled Force points towards the wall at its top; the wall is labelled Wall.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.1: A boy pushing a wall (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.1).

blocks.text: The force applied on a body may not always be in the direction of force as shown in Fig. (4.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints “in the direction of force”. It means the direction of displacement: the force applied on a body may not always be in the direction of its displacement, as in Fig. 4.2, where the rope pulls at an angle θ to the displacement d.

blocks.alt: A boy pulls a block with a rope. The block is shown at its starting position A and again at B to the right. From the block, the force arrow F runs along the rope at an angle theta above the horizontal displacement arrow d.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.2: A force F at an angle theta to the displacement d of a block pulled from A to B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.2).

blocks.text: If the force F makes an angle θ with the displacement d, the work done is equal to the product of the component of force along the direction of the displacement and the magnitude of displacement. Then

blocks.text_alt: W = (F cos θ) d = Fd cos θ   (4.2)

blocks.alt: Axes with F upward and d to the right. A vector F starts at the origin at an angle theta above the d-axis. A dashed line drops from its tip to the d-axis, and the arrow along the d-axis from the origin to that point is labelled F cos theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.3: The component F cos theta of the force F along the displacement d (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.3).

blocks.text: Equation (4.3) shows that work is a scalar quantity. The unit of work is joule (J). From Eq. (4.1), we have

When a constant force acts through a distance d, the event can be plotted on a simple graph (Fig. 4.4). The distance is normally plotted along x-axis and the force along y-axis. As the force does not vary, in this case, the graph will be a horizontal straight line. If the constant force F (newton) and the displacement d (metre) are in the same direction, then the work done is Fd (joule). Clearly shaded area in Fig. 4.4 is also Fd. Hence, the area under a force-displacement curve can be taken as to represent the work done by the constant force. In case the force F is not in the direction of displacement, the graph is plotted between F cos θ and d.

blocks.alt: A graph with Force on the y-axis and distance on the x-axis. A shaded rectangle OPQR: O at the origin, P on the y-axis, Q above R, R on the x-axis. A double arrow F beside QR gives its height and a double arrow d below gives OR.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.4: Force-distance graph of a constant force: the rectangle OPQR (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.4).

blocks.text: From the definition of work, we find that:

items: If θ < 90°, work is done and it is said to be positive work.
If θ = 90°, no work is done.
If θ > 90°, the work done is said to be negative.
SI unit of work is N m known as joule (J).
